title: Lowy's power index, Geelong's corpse flower and Wong's AI warning

stories.headline: US–China power gap in Asia at its narrowest, Lowy report finds
stories.headlineZh: 洛伊研究所报告：美中在亚洲的实力差距降至历史最小
stories.summaryZh: 洛伊研究所2026年亚洲实力指数显示，美国外交影响力创纪录下滑，中国稳步追赶，澳大利亚跌至第六。
stories.c1:
The United States has lost a considerable amount of power and influence in Asia over the past year, while China has steadily gained ground, according to the Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index. The annual report found that the overall gap between the two superpowers has shrunk to 5.3 points, the narrowest margin since the index was launched, although Washington still holds a clear lead.

The most striking shift came in diplomatic influence, where the US suffered a record decline. The report attributes much of this to the Trump administration's war with Iran and a string of unpopular policy decisions. Lead author Jack Sato identified three factors: a series of missteps by an increasingly transactional America, conflicts elsewhere diverting its attention away from the Indo-Pacific, and China's rapid military build-up. As a result, the American lead in military capability has narrowed from 27 points in 2018 to just over 15.

China, by contrast, held steady on most measures and now ranks first for both economic relationships and diplomatic influence. The two powers are almost level on economic capability in the region. Further down the table, India climbed to third place, consolidating its status as a major power, even though China's overall power is still 80 per cent greater.

For Australia, the picture is less encouraging. Its overall score dipped slightly and it slipped one place to sixth, behind Russia. South-East Asia was also hit hard by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which pushed up fuel and fertiliser prices, and diplomatic influence fell in almost every country in the region. Indonesia suffered the steepest drop, which the authors put down largely to its president's "haphazard" approach to foreign policy.
stories.b2:
A new report says the United States has lost a lot of power and influence in Asia this year, while China has moved closer. The Lowy Institute's 2026 Asia Power Index found that the overall gap between the two countries is now 5.3 points. This is the smallest gap since the index began, but the US is still clearly ahead.

The biggest change was in diplomatic influence, where the US had a record fall. The report links this to the war with Iran and other unpopular decisions by the Trump administration. Lead author Jack Sato said the US had made several mistakes, had been distracted by conflicts in other regions and had faced fast military growth in China. The US military lead has fallen from 27 points in 2018 to just over 15.

China stayed steady on most measures. It is now first for economic relationships and diplomatic influence, and the two powers are almost equal in economic capability. India rose to third place, although China is still 80 per cent more powerful.

Australia's score fell slightly, and it dropped one place to sixth, behind Russia. In South-East Asia, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz raised fuel and fertiliser prices. Indonesia had the biggest fall in diplomatic influence.

stories.headline: Scientists bank Geelong corpse flower's pollen to fight extinction
stories.headlineZh: 科学家采集吉朗尸花花粉入库，助力对抗物种灭绝
stories.summaryZh: 吉朗植物园的巨魔芋“皮特”开花后，研究人员首次将其花粉存入维州种子库，以防这一濒危物种灭绝。
stories.c1:
For a few days last week, thousands of people queued to squeeze into a steamy greenhouse at the Geelong Botanic Gardens, where the temperature is kept at around 27°C. The attraction was a titan arum, better known as the corpse flower, which its keepers had nicknamed "Pete". The plant is notorious for its pungent odour, which one local visitor likened to a teenage boy's school bag. By Friday morning, however, its brief moment of glory was over and the bloom had collapsed.

Behind the scenes, scientists were seizing a rare opportunity. Dr Rebecca Miller, a research scientist at Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria, monitored the plant's condition and temperature before cutting a small window into its base and collecting pollen with a scalpel. It is the first time corpse flower pollen has been stored at the Victorian Conservation Seedbank in Melbourne, where it is intended to serve as an insurance policy against extinction.

The stakes are high. Fewer than 1,000 titan arums are thought to survive in the wild, in the jungles of Indonesia, where they are threatened by poaching, climate change and the clearing of forests for palm oil, timber and agriculture. Their biology does not help either: each plant blooms for no more than two days, and only once every seven to ten years, so chances to pollinate are few and far between.

Miller will trial storage at minus 20 and minus 80 degrees Celsius, with varying levels of moisture, hoping to keep the pollen usable for a few years so that it can pollinate flowers in other botanic gardens. She concedes that viability may be low, but remains cautiously optimistic. She also hopes the attention will spill over to Australia's own under-appreciated arums, including a species from northern Australia that mimics dung to attract flies.
stories.b2:
Last week, thousands of people waited in line to enter a hot, humid greenhouse at the Geelong Botanic Gardens. They came to see a titan arum, also called the corpse flower, which staff had named "Pete". The plant is famous for its terrible smell. One visitor said it smelt like a teenage boy's school bag. By Friday morning, the flower had finished and collapsed.

While visitors enjoyed the show, scientists were busy. Dr Rebecca Miller from Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria checked the plant's condition, cut a small window into its base and collected pollen. This is the first time corpse flower pollen has been stored at the Victorian Conservation Seedbank in Melbourne. The idea is to protect the species from extinction.

The species is in serious danger. Fewer than 1,000 plants are believed to be left in the wild, in Indonesia's jungles. They face poaching, climate change and forest clearing. Each plant flowers for only up to two days, once every seven to ten years.

Miller will test storing the pollen at minus 20 and minus 80 degrees Celsius. She hopes it will stay usable for a few years, so other botanic gardens can use it. She admits it may not work well, but she is hopeful.

stories.discuss: Why do you think rare events like a corpse flower blooming attract such huge crowds? Can public curiosity really help protect endangered species?

stories.headline: Penny Wong to frame AI as a major national security challenge
stories.headlineZh: 黄英贤将把人工智能定位为重大国家安全挑战
stories.summaryZh: 外长黄英贤将在议会发表重要外交演讲，警告人工智能让外国干预更快更隐蔽，并呼吁澳大利亚迅速行动。
stories.c1:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong is set to put artificial intelligence at the centre of Australia's foreign policy, using a major speech to parliament on Tuesday to describe it as a significant national security challenge. The address, titled "Securing Australia's future in a changing world", will take the place of a foreign policy white paper. The last such document was published in 2017, and Wong has previously argued that these papers quickly become outdated.

In the speech, Wong will argue that AI is transforming military power and reshaping economies in ways that cannot be fully anticipated. She will also warn that the technology is making foreign interference faster, cheaper and harder to spot. She is expected to cite reports of an Iranian operation that used fake journalist personas to publish articles about the US-Iran conflict, as well as Russian covert operations that reportedly used deepfakes to sway US elections.

Her remarks come amid growing concern about the security of AI infrastructure at home. ASIO chief Mike Burgess warned that foreign adversaries could covertly seek some form of control over AI infrastructure, and that building data centres in Australia carries a risk of foreign interference. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has said such facilities act as a magnet for foreign interference and that their ownership structures warrant careful scrutiny.

Rather than waiting for international treaties, Wong will contend that Australia must act quickly, noting that it is already legislating mandatory AI safety standards and strengthening its cyber resilience. She will also caution that the race to develop frontier AI, concentrated in a handful of companies and countries, should not reward speed at the expense of prudence. Pointing to Australia's past influence on nuclear proliferation and online safety, she will signal an ambition to shape the rules on AI in a similar way.
stories.b2:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong will give an important speech to parliament on Tuesday. In it, she will describe artificial intelligence as a major national security challenge for Australia. The speech is called "Securing Australia's future in a changing world", and it will replace a foreign policy white paper. Australia's last white paper came out in 2017.

Wong will say that AI is changing military power, people's lives and the economy in ways that are hard to predict. She will also warn that AI makes foreign interference faster, cheaper and more difficult to notice. She is expected to mention reports that Iran used fake journalists to publish articles, and that Russia used deepfakes to try to influence US elections.

There are also worries about AI data centres in Australia. The head of ASIO, Mike Burgess, has warned that foreign enemies could try to secretly gain some control over AI infrastructure. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said data centres attract foreign interference, so their owners must be checked carefully.

Wong will argue that Australia should not wait for international agreements. She will say Australia is already making laws for AI safety standards. She will also warn that companies racing to build powerful AI should not put speed ahead of safety.

stories.headline: Is convenience making us lonelier? A journalist makes the case
stories.headlineZh: 便利让我们更孤独吗？一位记者这样认为
stories.summaryZh: 美国记者布拉德在新书《反对便利》中指出，应用程序和自助服务虽省时，却让人更孤立，并带来隐性代价。
stories.c1:
Ordering coffee through an app, streaming music and gliding through self-service checkouts may save us a few minutes, but according to American journalist Gabe Bullard, these everyday conveniences come at a hidden cost. In his book Against Convenience, Bullard, who lives in Switzerland, argues that many services designed to make life easier are quietly leaving us more isolated, while low-paid workers and the environment bear much of the burden.

His interest in the subject grew out of personal experience. After the pandemic lockdowns, he got into the habit of ordering his coffee ahead through an app, and found the routine surprisingly lonely. When he switched to a coffee shop where he had to order in person, and started inviting colleagues along, he noticed that his mood and his working relationships improved, and that the coffee was better too.

Bullard's broader point is that the less we leave home and deal with other people, the more isolated we become. He also worries that algorithmic feeds and personalised services, which cater to our individual tastes, may distort our sense of a shared world that none of us fully controls. A psychologist quoted in the interview makes a similar case: even waving at a stranger acknowledges that we occupy a shared space, and social skills tend to weaken when they go unused.

That is not to say Bullard rejects technology outright. Instead, he suggests that a little friction can be valuable, prompting us to reflect on what we consume. He now shops in stores rather than online, buys music instead of streaming it and chats more with strangers. He admits he was initially sceptical of one Swiss trend, in which people meet in parks to eat pudding with forks, but has come to see it as an encouraging way to socialise.
stories.b2:
Apps, streaming and fast self-service checkouts can save us time. But American journalist Gabe Bullard believes these conveniences have a hidden cost. In his book Against Convenience, he argues that many services which make life easier are also making us more isolated. He also says that low-paid workers and the environment often pay the price.

Bullard's idea came from his own life. After the pandemic lockdowns, he ordered his coffee through an app every day, and he felt lonely. Then he started going to a coffee shop where he ordered in person, and he invited colleagues to join him. His mood got better, he became closer to his colleagues, and even the coffee tasted better.

He believes that the less we go out and talk to people, the more alone we feel. He also thinks personalised feeds and services, which are designed around our own tastes, can change how we see the shared world. A psychologist in the interview agrees that small actions, like waving at a stranger, matter, and that social skills get weaker if we don't use them.

Bullard does not hate technology. He now shops in stores, buys music instead of streaming it, and talks more to strangers.

questions.explain: 原文 he noticed that his mood and his working relationships improved，与题干一致。

stories.discuss: Why do you think so many people choose convenience over contact with others? Do you think this trend will reverse in the future?

dialogue.title: Stuck at Richmond Station
dialogue.setting: Two colleagues are waiting on a crowded platform at Richmond station after their train home is delayed on a Monday evening.
dialogue.settingZh: 周一傍晚，两位同事回家的火车晚点，他们在拥挤的里士满车站站台上等车。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Don't tell me — the Frankston line's delayed again? That's the third time this week.
lines.zh: 别告诉我——弗兰克斯顿线又晚点了？这周已经第三次了。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Yep, signal fault near South Yarra, apparently. They're saying twenty minutes, at least.
lines.zh: 是啊，据说南亚拉附近信号故障。说至少要二十分钟。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Brilliant. I was hoping to squeeze in a run before dinner.
lines.zh: 太好了（反话）。我本来还想在晚饭前抽空跑个步。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Could be worse. At least it's not pouring like last Thursday.
lines.zh: 还不算最糟。至少不像上周四那样下倾盆大雨。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: True. I suppose I could just grab an Uber, but that'd cost a fortune at this hour.
lines.zh: 也是。我也可以叫个优步，但这个点会贵得离谱。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Funny, I was reading this morning about how convenience is making us lonelier.
lines.zh: 真巧，我今天早上刚读到一篇文章，说便利让我们更孤独。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Oh yeah? So you reckon a delayed train is good for the soul?
lines.zh: 哦是吗？所以你觉得火车晚点对心灵有好处？

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Sort of! We wouldn't be having a proper chat if we were stuck in separate cars.
lines.zh: 有点吧！如果我们各自坐在车里，就不会这样好好聊天了。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Fair point. I've barely spoken to anyone outside the office in weeks.
lines.zh: 有道理。我已经好几周几乎没和办公室以外的人说过话了。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Same here. Most days I just put my headphones in and zone out.
lines.zh: 我也是。大多数时候我就戴上耳机发呆。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: Hang on, is that our train? No — it's the Sandringham one. False alarm.
lines.zh: 等等，那是我们的车吗？不是——是桑德林厄姆线的。虚惊一场。

lines.name: Tom
lines.en: Tell you what, if it's not here in ten, let's grab a bite nearby.
lines.zh: 这样吧，如果十分钟内车还不来，我们就去附近随便吃点东西。

lines.name: Priya
lines.en: You're on. Dumplings on Swan Street? My shout, since you kept me sane.
lines.zh: 一言为定。去天鹅街吃饺子？我请客，谢谢你让我没崩溃。
